The Bluespotted trevally Caranx bucculentus exhibits early developmental milestones tightly coupled to ambient thermal conditions, with embryos incubated at 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C] completing eclosion after just 7 days [ab = 7 days]. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva carries a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.000523 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000523 grams], a mass derived from a fertilised ovum roughly 1 millimeter in diameter. This lecithotrophic stage relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves, and the rapid absorption of these nutrients during the first week post-hatching is critical for the onset of exogenous feeding. Field observations indicate that the transition from endotrophic to exotrophic nutrition typically coincides with complete yolk-sac resorption, after which the actively growing pelagic larva must encounter suitable zooplankton prey to sustain further development. The brevity of this initial phase underscores the species' reliance on warm, productive coastal waters during the spawning season, as cooler temperatures would prolong the egg stage and potentially reduce larval survival by delaying the point at which first feeding becomes possible.

As the planktonic larva progresses through its pelagic phase, somatic growth proceeds rapidly under the warm thermal regime typical of its nursery habitats. The juvenile stage begins after a pronounced larval metamorphosis, during which the body plan undergoes an allometric shift and the developing fish settles into shallow coastal environments. By the time individuals reach puberty, which occurs when they attain a total length at puberty of 11 centimeters [Lp = 11 centimeters], their body mass has increased substantially from the neonatal condition. The wet weight at puberty has been estimated at 27.5 grams [Wwp = 27.5 grams], reflecting the considerable investment in somatic tissue required before the onset of gonadal maturation. This size threshold appears to be a robust indicator of reproductive readiness across the species' geographic range, and individuals below this length are rarely observed in a gravid state during field surveys. The consistency of this relationship between length and maturity suggests that the onset of gametogenesis is closely tied to achieving a critical body size rather than a fixed chronological age, a pattern common among fast-growing tropical carangids.

The maximum total length attained by Caranx bucculentus has been documented at 66 centimeters [Li = 66 centimeters], representing the ultimate total length reached by the largest individuals in wild populations corresponding to an asymptotic body size of approximately 5000 grams [Wwi = approximately 5000 grams]. This substantial adult mass, which is more than nine million times greater than the initial egg weight, illustrates the extraordinary scope for post-settlement growth in this species. Examination of length-frequency distributions from commercial catches suggests that most individuals approach this asymptotic size within a few years of reaching maturity, after which further increases in length are minimal. The rapid attainment of near-maximum dimensions is consistent with the life history strategy of an iteroparous predator that occupies a high trophic position in pelagic food webs. Interestingly, the relationship between length and weight follows a power-law function typical of fusiform carangids, with the ultimate wet weight reflecting the energetic demands of maintaining a large, active body capable of sustained swimming and predation.

Reproductive output in Bluespotted trevally is tied to both body size and environmental temperature. Under the warm conditions prevalent in their tropical range (27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]), the maximum lifespan for this species is estimated at 5 years [am = 5 years], a relatively short generation time consistent with a fast life history pace. This longevity constraint means that individuals must allocate resources efficiently between somatic growth and reproduction across a compressed reproductive window. Age-based analyses of otoliths from wild-caught fish support this lifespan estimate, with very few individuals exceeding five years in age even in lightly exploited populations. The combination of rapid early growth, early maturity at a modest size, and a short maximum lifespan aligns with expectations for a species that experiences high natural mortality rates, particularly during the vulnerable larval and early juvenile stages. This life history strategy appears to be an adaptation to productive but unpredictable coastal environments where the ability to reproduce quickly and repeatedly confers a selective advantage.

Comparative life history data place Caranx bucculentus among the faster-growing members of the Carangidae, with its early maturity at 11 centimeters total length and its ultimate size of 66 centimeters being intermediate within the genus. The wet weight at puberty of 27.5 grams represents only a small fraction of the 5000 grams ultimate wet weight, indicating that individuals invest heavily in growth after reaching maturity. This pattern is energetically sensible for a predator that must quickly achieve a body size sufficient to exploit larger prey items and to avoid gape-limited predation. The maximum recorded lifespan of 5 years under natural conditions is notably shorter than that reported for some larger carangids, which may exceed 20 years in cooler waters, but is comparable to that of other small-to-medium-sized tropical trevallies. The near-constant thermal regime in the species' core distribution likely accelerates physiological processes across all life stages, compressing the time available for growth and reproduction while imposing a metabolic ceiling on maximum longevity. Future work should examine how fine-scale temperature variation within nursery habitats influences growth trajectories and the timing of key life history transitions.
